summary: The article argues that culinary arts festivals deserve recognition alongside traditional art forms, asking why chefs are rarely given the same reverence as painters or sculptors. It surveys upcoming fall 2023 festivals, including The Epicurean Canvas, Fusion Mosaic, Root & Marrow and Spice Symphony, and describes how they combine innovation, sensory spectacle, heritage and sustainability. It closes with open questions rather than a firm verdict on whether food sits beside a Caravaggio or a Warhol.
one_line: Culinary arts festivals in fall 2023 prompt the question of whether chefs' creations deserve a place alongside painting, sculpture and other traditional art forms.
key_facts: The Epicurean Canvas is scheduled for the second weekend of September 2023 in the heart of downtown gastronomy.
The Epicurean Canvas is organized by food critic Esther Robinson and Michelin-starred chef Julian Lefebvre.

The Epicurean Canvas aims to challenge preconceptions about what food can be, asking whether a chef's manipulation of flavors, textures and presentation should weigh as much as an artist's manipulation of paint and clay.
Fusion Mosaic runs from October 15th to the 17th and is spearheaded by restaurateur Meena Choi.
Fusion Mosaic is a tribute to the melting pot of contemporary society, blending disparate culinary traditions into harmonious dishes.
Root & Marrow is set for late September and is curated by environmental advocate George Bennett and a team of ecoconscious chefs.
Root & Marrow highlights heirloom recipes and indigenous ingredients and promotes culinary conservation.
Sous-vide virtuoso Lila Ramirez is cited as a chef who takes the spotlight and proclaims her cooking philosophy to an engrossed crowd.
Spice Symphony is upcoming in November, where chef-artist Anaya Patel plans a series of courses paired with an original score composed solely for the menu.
The article says culinary art is often relegated to craft rather than fine art, possibly because of its transient nature or its role in basic sustenance.
The festivals feature live demonstrations, pop-up kitchens and aromas, with chefs described as conductors of an edible orchestra.
The article ends by asking whether a salad can be placed beside a Caravaggio or a Warhol, leaving the question open.
